sentence: Each string is just under a meter, as in a grandfather clock.
claim: A seconds pendulum (one second per swing) is 0.994 m long at standard gravity, and that length became the standard in quality long-case (grandfather) clocks.
note: Excerpt: 'a pendulum 0.994 m (39.1 in) long, in which each swing takes one second, became widely used in quality clocks'; at standard gravity ≈ 993.6 mm. Computed: L = g/π² = 9.81/9.8696 = 0.9940 m. The bench's strings are 99.4 cm to the bob's centre.

claim: A 0.994 m pendulum's small-swing period is T = 2π√(L/g) = 2.000 s, so one swing across (half a period) takes about 1 s; at this episode's 10° and 30° the exact half-periods are 1.002 s and 1.017 s.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 15.5 Pendulums (LibreTexts copy)
note: Excerpt: T = 2π√(L/g). Computed: 2π√(0.994/9.81) = 2.0000 s. Exact large-angle ratio 2K(sin(θ0/2))/π = 1.00191 at 10°, 1.01741 at 30° (the AGM; checked against arXiv:physics/0510206's exact period).

sentence: Ghosts every tenth of a second bunch up at the turns.
claim: Without losses, a pendulum's kinetic energy is zero at the turning points and greatest at the bottom, so equal-time ghosts crowd together near the ends of the swing and spread out at the bottom.
note: Excerpt: at the highest point the kinetic energy equals 0 and the potential energy is maximum; at the lowest point the kinetic energy is at its maximum. The ghosts are the scene's exact positions every 0.1 s.

sentence: Three times the distance… and still, neck and neck.
claim: Released together from 30° and 10°, two identical 0.994 m pendulums reach the bottom 7.8 ms apart (quarter periods 0.5087 s and 0.5010 s): the 30° swing's arc is exactly three times longer.
source_title: F. M. S. Lima & P. Arun, An accurate formula for the period of a simple pendulum oscillating beyond the small-angle regime, Am. J. Phys. 74(10), 892 (2006) (arXiv:physics/0510206)
note: Computed from the exact period: T0·(1.01741 − 1.00191)/4 = 2.0000 × 0.0155 / 4 = 7.75 ms. Arc length = L·θ0, so 30° against 10° is exactly 3×. 'Neck and neck' (close, not tied) on purpose: the measure segment shows the gap growing. Source title corrected on 26 Oct (the audit found the earlier title was not the paper's): search excerpt of the arXiv record gives Lima & Arun's title and Am. J. Phys. 2006; its formula is checked against the exact elliptic-integral period these numbers come from.

sentence: Galileo claimed every swing takes the same time, wide or narrow.
claim: Galileo claimed the pendulum is isochronous: its period does not depend on the size of the arc (in a 1602 letter and in Two New Sciences, for all arcs under 180°).
source_title: Paolo Palmieri, A phenomenology of Galileo's experiments with pendulums, British Journal for the History of Science (author's copy, University of Pittsburgh)
note: Excerpts (Palmieri; also Cambridge Core, https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-for-the-history-of-science/article/phenomenology-of-galileos-experiments-with-pendulums/494C00BA710DB3244C683CDE216457B9): 'his claim that the pendulum was isochronous for all arcs less than 180° has created something of a puzzle'; 'Galileo claims that all pendulums are isochronous in an 1602 letter, but failed to demonstrate it'. Two New Sciences also reports comparing leaden balls drawn aside about 80° and 4–5° (search excerpts of the Fourth Day; the excerpts disagree on its wording, so it is not said on air).

sentence: For small swings, he was nearly right.
claim: For small swings (especially below about 15°) the period is nearly independent of amplitude, so Galileo's claim is nearly right there; larger swings take measurably longer (13.7% at 80°).
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 15.5 Pendulums (LibreTexts copy)
note: OpenStax University Physics 15.5 (15.4 on openstax.org; the LibreTexts copy, as c2): the period 'is nearly independent of amplitude, especially if θ is less than about 15°'. The 13.7% at 80° is computed from the exact period: 2K(sin 40°)/π = 1.1375 (Lima & Arun, c11's source). Repointed on 26 Oct (audit): the earlier main link was an IB student paper (arXiv:1805.00002).

sentence: Three times farther out, the pull is almost three times stronger.
claim: The restoring force along the arc is mg·sin θ: at 30° it is 2.88 times that at 10° ('almost three times').
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 15.5 Pendulums (LibreTexts copy)
note: Excerpt (OpenStax 15.5): the restoring force is −mg sin θ, about −mgθ for small angles. Computed: sin 30°/sin 10° = 0.5/0.1736 = 2.88. 'The pull' is gravity's component along the arc; gravity itself is the same.

sentence: So it covers triple the path at nearly triple the speed: nearly the same time.
claim: For small swings the restoring force is nearly proportional to the displacement (simple harmonic motion), so the period nearly does not depend on the amplitude; because the pull grows a little slower than the distance (sin θ < θ), the bigger swing is slightly slower.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 15.5 Pendulums (LibreTexts copy)
note: Excerpt: 'For small displacements, a pendulum is identical to a simple harmonic oscillator', and 'the period of a pendulum is nearly independent of amplitude'. Computed: the bottom speed 2√(gL)·sin(θ0/2) is 2.97× larger at 30° than at 10° (1.62 against 0.54 m/s), over an arc exactly 3× longer. The measure segment gives the exact shortfall (c11, c12).

sentence: Now hang fifteen, each a little shorter.
claim: A simple pendulum's period depends only on its length and g, not on its mass, so fifteen pendulums of different lengths (and the same start angle) swing at fifteen different rates.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 15.5 Pendulums (LibreTexts copy)
note: Excerpt (OpenStax 15.5 adaptation): 'the only things that affect the period of a simple pendulum are its length and the acceleration due to gravity. The period is completely independent of other factors, such as mass.' (Amplitude: c6.) The bench's fifteen run 34.4 cm down to 21.2 cm.

claim: The fifteen pendulums differ only in length (same bobs, same 12° start), and length is what sets a pendulum's period, so each swings at its own rate.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 15.5 Pendulums (LibreTexts copy)
note: Same excerpt as c9 ('the only things that affect the period of a simple pendulum are its length and the acceleration due to gravity'). The bench's fifteen share bob, start angle and g. The bench's fifteen start at 15°.

sentence: For half a minute, they drift apart.
claim: Fifteen uncoupled pendulums tuned so the longest makes 51 back-and-forth swings in 60 s and each shorter one makes one more, up to 65, fall out of step for the first 30 s (neighbours swing on opposite sides at 30 s).
source_title: Harvard Natural Sciences Lecture Demonstrations, Pendulum Waves
note: Excerpt: 'The length of the longest pendulum has been adjusted so that it executes 51 oscillations in this 60 second period. Thus, the 15th pendulum (shortest) undergoes 65 oscillations.' Computed lengths L = g(T/2π)², T = 60/(51 + n): 34.39 cm … 21.17 cm.  Corrected on 26 Oct (audit): the pattern is symmetric about the half-minute: each pendulum's x_n(60 − t) = x_n(t), so the drift apart lasts 30 s and the second half retraces it. Harvard excerpt: 'at 30 seconds, half of the pendulums are at one amplitude maximum and the other half are at the opposite amplitude maximum'.

sentence: Then, just as gradually… back in line.
claim: Over the second half they retrace the first half in reverse and are back in line at the end of the 60 s cycle: in 60 s each has made a whole number of back-and-forth swings (51 … 65).
source_title: Harvard Natural Sciences Lecture Demonstrations, Pendulum Waves
note: Same Harvard excerpt as c10. Computed: the bench's fifteen start at 15°, which lengthens every period by the same 0.43% (exact ratio 1.00430), so they realign at 60 × 1.00430 = 60.26 s (compile.py WAVE_TH, film.json wave.align 60.258). Shown fast, with the speed note. 'Just as gradually': x_n(60 − t) = x_n(t) (corrected on 26 Oct; the line had said 'all at once').

sentence: Measure it: twenty swings, and the big one is three tenths of a second behind.
claim: Twenty swings (ten periods) take 20.35 s at 30° and 20.04 s at 10° for a 0.994 m pendulum: the big swing falls 0.31 s behind.
source_title: F. M. S. Lima & P. Arun, An accurate formula for the period of a simple pendulum oscillating beyond the small-angle regime, Am. J. Phys. 74(10), 892 (2006) (arXiv:physics/0510206)
note: Computed from the exact period T = T0 · 2K(sin(θ0/2))/π, T0 = 2.0000 s: 10 × 2.0000 × (1.01741 − 1.00191) = 0.310 s. A 'swing' is one way across, as a clock counts it. Source title corrected on 26 Oct (the audit found the earlier title was not the paper's): search excerpt of the arXiv record gives Lima & Arun's title and Am. J. Phys. 2006; its formula is checked against the exact elliptic-integral period these numbers come from.

sentence: At thirty degrees, Galileo is off by about one part in sixty.
claim: A 30° swing's period is 1.74% longer than the small-swing value 2π√(L/g), about one part in 57, so at 30° the claim of equal times is off by about one part in sixty.
source_title: F. M. S. Lima & P. Arun, An accurate formula for the period of a simple pendulum oscillating beyond the small-angle regime, Am. J. Phys. 74(10), 892 (2006) (arXiv:physics/0510206)
note: Computed: exact ratio 1.01741 (the arithmetic-geometric mean form of K; the bible's figure, 1.7% at 30°). 1/0.01741 = 57.4: 'one part in sixty' rounds it. Galileo's claim covered every arc under 180°; the line limits itself to this swing. Source title corrected on 26 Oct (the audit found the earlier title was not the paper's): search excerpt of the arXiv record gives Lima & Arun's title and Am. J. Phys. 2006; its formula is checked against the exact elliptic-integral period these numbers come from.

claim: A simple pendulum's period is set by its length (and g): T = 2π√(L/g).
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 15.5 Pendulums (LibreTexts copy)

sentence: A wider swing just moves faster: almost fast enough.
claim: A wider swing reaches a higher speed (2.97× at 30° against 10°) over a path 3× longer, so it takes only slightly longer: 1.55% for 30° against 10°.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 15.5 Pendulums (LibreTexts copy)
note: Computed: c7, c11. Said under the 'Ideal pendulums: no air, no friction' note.

claim: A dropped tennis ball comes back well under the height it fell from (the ITF test: from 254 cm onto concrete, a rebound of 135–147 cm), so it never returns to the hand that dropped it.
source_title: Tennis Warehouse University, ball testing (ITF rebound range)
note: Excerpt: dropped from 100 in (254 cm) onto concrete, an approved ball rebounds 53–58 in (135–147 cm), 53–58% of the drop. Repointed on 26 Oct (audit): the earlier McMaster citation's excerpt came from a related search, not that page. Episode 3's c1 uses the same source.
